summary: Defines MIB textual conventions for representing URIs so that other MIB modules can import them instead of defining their own. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A shared template for writing web addresses in network monitoring data.

questions: what is a uri textual convention
what is the difference between uri255 and uri1024
how are uris normalized in a mib
subtitle: Three shared MIB data types for writing URIs, so every MIB module does not invent its own.

tldr.problem: MIB modules that need to hold a URI would otherwise each define their own representation, which hurts compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: A new MIB module, URI-TC-MIB, defines three textual conventions: Uri (unlimited length), Uri255 (up to 255 octets) and Uri1024 (up to 1024 octets). Values must be US-ASCII and normalized.
tldr.outcome: Other MIB modules import these conventions instead of defining their own. The module defines no managed objects itself.

today: RFC 5017 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) used with network management protocols. It defines textual conventions for representing URIs as defined in STD 66 (RFC 3986), which are further described by RFC 3305.

Three conventions are defined: one of unlimited length and two of different restricted lengths. Which length fits depends on tradeoffs in the particular MIB module. Providing standard restricted-length conventions is meant to improve compatibility between MIB modules that need restricted-length URIs.

The intent, from the abstract, is that these conventions will be imported by MIB modules that would otherwise define their own representations.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone drawing their own box for a web address, there is now a standard box in three sizes that everybody can copy.

sections.title: The Management Framework Behind It
sections.content:
The RFC fits into the Internet-Standard Management Framework, which RFC 3410 describes. Managed objects are held in a virtual information store called the MIB, and are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

Objects in the MIB are defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is compliant with SMIv2, described in STD 58 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).
sections.eli5: Network devices keep a big list of facts about themselves. This document adds one more kind of entry to that list's rulebook.

sections.title: The Three Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module URI-TC-MIB is rooted at { mib-2 164 }. It defines three conventions, all built on OCTET STRING.

  • Uri: no length restriction, display hint 1a.
  • Uri255: size 0 to 255, display hint 255a.
  • Uri1024: size 0 to 1024, display hint 1024a.

All three share the same rules for content, described in the next section. Their descriptions note that STD 66 URIs are of unlimited length, so objects using the restricted forms impose a limit on what they can represent. Where no limit is needed, objects SHOULD use Uri.
sections.eli5: There are three boxes: a stretchy one, a medium one and a larger one. Pick the stretchy one unless you really need a size limit.

sections.title: Rules for URI Values
sections.content:
Objects using these conventions MUST use US-ASCII encoding and MUST be normalized as described in Sections 6.2.1, 6.2.2.1 and 6.2.2.2 of RFC 3986. Unnecessary percent-encoding is removed, and case-insensitive characters are set to lowercase, except hexadecimal digits, which are normalized to uppercase.

The purpose is to help provide unique URIs, but the RFC says the normalization is not sufficient: two URIs that differ textually after normalization may still be equivalent.

Objects MAY restrict the schemes they permit; the text notes that data: and urn: might not be appropriate. A zero-length URI is not a valid URI, which can be used to express 'URI absent', for example in an index field.
sections.eli5: Everyone must write the address the same tidy way, with the same capital and small letters, so two copies of the same address look alike. That helps, but it cannot catch every case.

sections.title: Indexing, Security and IANA
sections.content:
If a URI is used as an index object, the Uri convention SHOULD be subtyped to a length appropriate for the Object Identifier (OID) it is part of. The description adds that an OID has an absolute limit of 128 subids, and that it is not efficient to have OIDs whose length approaches this limit.

The module defines no management objects, only a convention that others may import. The RFC therefore says meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define objects, and that this document has no impact on the security of the Internet. It also points to the security considerations of STD 66.

IANA assigned { mib-2 164 } to the URI-TC-MIB module.
sections.eli5: If the address is used as a filing label, keep it short so the label does not get too long. The document itself holds no secrets, so it adds no new security worries.
